Components in a Circuit: Passive, Active, Rectifiers, and Reading the Schematic

Unit 4: Electricity, Electronics, and Imaging Power. Lesson 15 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Open an imaging generator and you see the same two dozen electronic components over and over. Knowing what each one does, and what each one does when it fails, is most of electronic troubleshooting.

Passive components

  • Resistors limit current and drop voltage. In the filament circuit they set the milliampere stations, so a drifted resistor or a dirty tap is a linearity problem.
  • Capacitors store charge. They pass alternating current and block direct current, smooth rectified voltage, and in a capacitor-discharge portable they are the exposure energy itself. Treat every one as charged until you have discharged it with the manufacturer's tool and read zero.
  • Inductors oppose a change in current: chokes, stator windings, and the windings of every transformer.
  • Transformers at component level are two coupled windings that change alternating voltage by their turns ratio.

The RC time constant

A capacitor charging through a resistor fills on a curve, not instantly. One time constant is tau = R x C: a capacitor reaches about 63 percent of the final voltage in one time constant and is essentially full, about 99 percent, after five. A 10 kohm resistor with a 100 microfarad capacitor gives tau = 1 second, so five seconds to full. The same curve runs backward on discharge, which is why a bleeder resistor's value tells you how long a cabinet needs before it is safe.

Active components

Diode        conducts one way; about 0.7 V forward drop in silicon; shorted passes both ways, open neither
Rectifier    half-wave passes one half-cycle, full-wave uses both, a bridge of four diodes is the usual form
Transistor   switches or amplifies on a small control current
SCR          a gate-triggered AC switch; the usual exposure and rotor switching element
Relay        a small coil current switching a large load; a contactor is a heavy-duty relay
Fuse, breaker opens on overcurrent; a repeat trip is a fault, never a nuisance

Relays, contactors, solenoids, brakes, and motors are the electromechanical devices in the cabinet: current moving metal. They fail mechanically rather than electrically, so they are the parts you expect to find pitted, burned, or sticking, and they are the ones a nose and a finger diagnose faster than a meter.

Rectification matters because the tube needs one-way current. Without it the negative half-cycle would drive electrons the wrong way and destroy the tube; with it, ripple falls as pulses per cycle rise, from 100 percent on single-phase to about 14 percent on six-pulse three-phase, 4 percent on twelve-pulse, and about 1 percent on a high-frequency generator.

Interlocks and indicators

An interlock is a contact in series with the exposure circuit: door, rotor ready, receptor parked, correct cassette size, collimator, emergency stop. Because they are in series, one open contact gives no exposure and very often no fault code, which is the classic "nothing happens" call. An indicator LED that is dark means the lamp or the circuit driving it is dead, so prove which before you conclude anything from it.

Reading an imaging schematic

Learn the schematic symbols first, because a drawing is unreadable without them: a resistor is a zigzag or a plain rectangle, a capacitor two parallel plates with one curved if it is polarized, an inductor or winding a coil, a transformer two coils with a core between them, a diode a triangle against a bar pointing the way current flows, a transistor a circle with three leads, a fuse a short link, and a contact a pair of lines that a coil symbol beside it operates. Then follow four paths, in this order:

  1. Power path: incoming supply, disconnect, main contactor, the autotransformer, the step-up transformer, rectifiers, and the tube.
  2. Control path: console, logic boards, the timer, and the exposure switch's two stages.
  3. Interlock chain: drawn as a string of normally open or normally closed contacts in series. Walk it contact by contact with the power off, on continuity.
  4. Test points: the manual marks them with the expected value. A test point that matches the printed value proves everything upstream of it; the first one that does not names the stage.
Exam tip: capacitors pass alternating current and block direct current, inductors do the opposite. Tau = R x C, 63 percent in one time constant and about 99 percent in five. Rectifiers exist because the tube needs direct current. Interlocks are in series, so one open contact gives no exposure and no code. Discharge before you touch.
Remember
Resistors drop voltage and set milliampere stations, capacitors store charge and pass alternating current, inductors oppose current change, and transformers change voltage by turns ratio; tau equals R times C gives 63 percent in one time constant and about 99 percent in five; diodes drop about 0.7 V and rectify half-wave, full-wave, or as a bridge so the tube gets one-way current, while transistors, SCRs, relays, contactors, fuses, and breakers switch and protect; and a schematic is read as power path, control path, interlock chain in series, and test points against their printed values.
Deeper explanation

Components in a Circuit: Passive, Active, Rectifiers, and Reading the Schematic, explained slowly

A small parts list, used over and over

An imaging generator looks complicated because it is large, not because it has many kinds of parts. Learn what each part does, what it does when it fails, and how it is drawn, and a schematic becomes readable.

The passive parts and their failure modes

Part        Does                              Fails as
Resistor    limits current, drops voltage,    open (no current), or drifted high (low mA,
            sets the mA stations              failed linearity); discolored or cracked
Capacitor   stores charge, passes AC, blocks  shorted (blows a fuse), open (ripple, resets),
            DC, smooths rectified voltage     leaking or bulging (the visible warning)
Inductor    opposes a change in current:      open winding (no rotor, no drive), shorted turns
            chokes, stator windings           (overheating, hum, nuisance trips)
Transformer two coupled windings changing     open or shorted winding, failed insulation,
            AC voltage by turns ratio         oil low or contaminated, arcing

A capacitor deserves the extra caution: in a capacitor-discharge portable it holds the exposure energy itself, and in any generator the smoothing and filter capacitors hold enough to hurt long after the disconnect is open. Discharge with the manufacturer's tool, to ground, and verify with a meter.

The RC time constant, and why you care

A capacitor charging through a resistor fills along a curve. One time constant is tau = R x C, and the curve is always the same shape:

After 1 tau     about 63 percent of the final voltage
After 2 tau     about 86 percent
After 3 tau     about 95 percent
After 5 tau     about 99 percent: treated as full
Discharge       the same curve downward, through the bleeder resistor
Worked          10 kohm x 100 microfarads = 10,000 x 0.0001 = 1 second, so about 5 seconds to full

The practical use is safety: the bleed-down time a service manual gives you is five time constants of the bleeder path, and it is the difference between a safe cabinet and a trip to the emergency department. The second use is timing: filter cutoffs, delay circuits, and charge times are all this curve in disguise.

The active parts

Part         Does                                     Fails as
Diode        conducts one way; about 0.7 V forward     shorted (conducts both ways, overcurrent
             drop in silicon                           fault), or open (half the waveform missing)
Rectifier    makes the one-way current the tube        one failed element: low output, high ripple,
             needs: half-wave, full-wave, bridge       a tube arc or overcurrent fault
Transistor   switches or amplifies on a small          shorted on, open off, or thermally
             control current                           intermittent
SCR          a gate-triggered AC switch, used in       shorted passes power continuously, open
             primary circuits and rotor drives         passes nothing; check both sides before
                                                       blaming the control board
Relay or     a small coil current switching a large    coil open, contacts pitted or welded,
contactor    load; a contactor is the heavy version    chatter from a weak coil supply
Fuse or      opens on overcurrent                      a repeat trip is a fault, never a nuisance
breaker

Rectification is not optional: without it the negative half-cycle would drive current backward through the tube and destroy it. As pulses per cycle rise, ripple falls, and ripple is image quality: 100 percent on single-phase, about 14 percent six-pulse, about 4 percent twelve-pulse, about 1 percent high-frequency. Less ripple means more output and a harder beam for the same settings, which is why one technique chart does not transfer between generator types.

The interlock chain, and why it hides

Interlocks are contacts in series with the exposure circuit: door, rotor ready, receptor parked and the right size, collimator, emergency stop, tube thermal. Because they are in series, one open contact produces no exposure and frequently no fault code at all, which is the classic "I press it and nothing happens" call. Walk the chain with the power off on continuity, contact by contact, from one end. An LED that is dark tells you either the lamp or its drive circuit is dead, so prove which before concluding anything from it.

Reading an imaging schematic

Path             Follow it from                       to                         Looking for
Power            disconnect, main contactor           autotransformer, step-up,  the first point with no
                                                      rectifier, tube            voltage
Control          console, logic boards, timer         the exposure contactor     a command that is sent
                                                                                 but not obeyed
Interlock chain  one end of the string                the other                  the open contact
Low voltage      each cabinet supply                  each board it feeds        a sagging rail
Test points      the manual's marked points           their printed values       the first mismatch

Test points are the whole reason a service manual is worth reading before you open anything: a point that reads its printed value proves everything upstream of it is working, so each measurement halves the problem.

What to memorize

  • Capacitors pass AC and block DC; inductors oppose a change in current.
  • Tau = R x C; 63 percent in one time constant, about 99 percent in five; bleed-down time is five time constants.
  • Silicon diode drops about 0.7 V; rectifiers exist because the tube needs DC; ripple 100, 14, 4, and about 1 percent.
  • Interlocks are in series: one open contact means no exposure and often no code.
  • Read a schematic as power path, control path, interlock chain, low-voltage rails, and test points.
